description:
We love to create/do stuff.

For NASA’s “Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map” challenge, we tackled one gap. Mars maps show the whole planet, but a walking astronaut needs the next 2 km: which ground is safe, how long walks take in a suit, and whether there’s enough oxygen to get back. ARIADNE turns real NASA data into a tablet map and helmet display that plans safe routes to science stops and draws the Thread, a live boundary of how far the astronaut can go and still return to the rover.
summary:
Imagine the first astronauts walking on Mars. They are there for science discovery, collecting samples and carrying tools in stiff spacesuits, with limited oxygen, steep broken ground and solar storms that strike without warning. Yet every Mars map today was made for planetary scientists, not for an explorer asking, "where can I safely go, how much science can I do, and can I still get home?"

We built ARIADNE, named after the thread that led Theseus out of the labyrinth. Our pipeline fuses real NASA data (HiRISE terrain, Curiosity weather, radiation and photos, CRISM minerals, THEMIS thermal inertia) into one map of a 2 km Marswalk in Gale Crater. On it we are building a planning table, a 3D view and a suit display. ARIADNE routes the crew through science stops, like Curiosity’s sulfur stones and boxwork ridges, each with its sampling task, while avoiding steep ground and large rocks. Walking times account for the suit and the load carried. The Thread marks how far the crew can go and still walk back to their rover, so they always know their remaining science time.

Exploration succeeds only when explorers return with discoveries. ARIADNE balances both at every step.
details:
What it does and how it works

ARIADNE (Astronaut Route Intelligence And Data for Navigation & Exploration) is a map and suit display for one astronaut on one Marswalk. It covers a 2 × 2 km patch of Gale Crater with two of Curiosity’s headline discoveries. The groundwater boxwork ridges and the pure sulfur stones of Gediz Vallis. It answers the astronaut’s three questions, "where can I safely go", "how much science can I do", and "can I still get home?"

It has two parts:

  • A Python pipeline: It runs once and offline. It turns real NASA data into one local metre grid, HiRISE 1 m terrain and 25 cm imagery, Curiosity REMS weather, RAD radiation and Navcam photos, CRISM minerals, and THEMIS thermal inertia. From these it works out:
    • slope, roughness and rocks (found from their shadows)
    • a walking-time cost for every cell, using Tobler’s hiking function scaled for a suit and capped at Apollo’s walking speed of about 1 m/s
    • a “return field”: How long it takes to walk back to the rover from anywhere.
    • Tablet (for the habitat or rover): A phosphor-hologram map with a 2D view and a 3D view. You plan the science stops, called Knots, here. Each Knot has real Curiosity photos and sampling tasks.
    • Visor (for inside the helmet): A first-person heads-up display with a compass, the next Knot and the oxygen left. It never shows more than three numbers.
    • The two displays sync in real time with no server.

At the centre is the Thread: A live boundary around everywhere the astronaut can still reach and walk back from in time. It shrinks as time passes and as heavy samples add load. In the demo run, a space weather watch gives a 30-minute countdown. Then a solar storm arrives, replayed from the real dose curve Curiosity measured in May 2024. The science plan stops, and the pressurized rover drives out to meet the astronaut halfway.

Benefits

  • Routes avoid ground that is no-go for a suited walker: Slopes above 25°, large rocks and rough terrain. On our patch, 18% of the ground is steeper than 25°.
  • Walking times account for the suit and the load being carried. Older field tools assume a constant walking speed.
  • Every alert comes with an action, such as “[ROUTE] to the rover”.
  • Every number shows where it came from: Dataset, product ID, resolution and uncertainty. Model-derived values are marked “est.”.
  • It works offline. Mars has no GPS and no cloud.

Intended impact

Every Mars map today is built for scientists studying a whole planet. We want to show what a map for the person standing on Mars looks like. It should balance science and getting home at every step, and replace the walk-back limits that Apollo ground teams worked out by hand. The same method works for any site with a HiRISE terrain model, and for Artemis Moon walks.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Pipeline: Python with uv, rasterio/GDAL, pyproj, numpy, scipy, scikit-image and pillow
  • App: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Three.js through React Three Fiber, Zustand, Tailwind CSS, d3-contour, Web Workers for A, Theta and D* Lite routing, and BroadcastChannel to sync the displays
  • Testing: pytest (68 tests), Vitest (414 tests) and a contract validator with 47 checks that keeps the pipeline and the app in agreement
  • Checks and hosting: QGIS for visual alignment checks, GitHub, and Vercel as a static host
  • Hardware: None beyond laptops. It runs in any browser. The total download is about 27 MB
  • AI assistance: Claude Code and opencode (DeepSeek) as coding agents

How it is creative

  • It turns a Greek mythology into a solution with an interface. The boxwork ridges are a natural labyrinth, and Ariadne’s thread becomes a live safe-return boundary.
  • The storm is real data based on the May 2024 solar particle event that Curiosity measured. The rescue is real Artemis-style planning, with the rover coming to meet the crew.
  • The look is a retro phosphor hologram, built for a glove-friendly and glanceable helmet display.
  • The tablet and visor sync without a server, account or network.

Factors the team considered

  • Safety first: No-go slope limits, a 30-minute oxygen reserve, Artemis 8-hour EVA planning, and Apollo suited walking speeds
  • Honesty: The data is replayed, not live, and the weather and the storm come from different dates. CRISM (18 m) and THEMIS (100 m) are shown as context only and never used for routing. We checked our terrain against reality, slopes from the terrain model match Curiosity’s own measured tilt at 205 stops (median 8.8° against 8.4°)
  • Usability: Large touch targets, at most three numbers on the visor, and alerts that always come with an action
  • Robustness and size: No backend, a small download, and automated tests and validation

Future plans, real deployment and scalability

  • Scalability: The pipeline runs once, offline, for any site with a HiRISE terrain model. Adding a new Marswalk only means choosing new map bounds and science stops and running the pipeline again. The app is a static site of about 27 MB with no server, so it can be copied onto a tablet or a suit computer and run without a network
  • Real deployment: Replace the replayed data with live feeds from sensors at the habitat and on the rover, plus space weather warnings relayed from Earth. Mars has no GPS, so the astronaut’s position would come from rover radio ranging, visual odometry or a future Mars navigation network instead of our simulation
  • Next steps: Support astronauts working in pairs, detect rocks with machine learning, test it with crews in analogue spacewalks on Earth, and adapt it for Artemis Moon walks using lunar terrain data from LRO
